clinicalPearls: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour arising most often in the gastrointestinal tract (notably small bowel, appendix and rectum) and the bronchopulmonary system; current WHO classifications increasingly use the term neuroendocrine tumour in place of carcinoid

Classified by embryological origin into foregut (bronchus, stomach, duodenum, pancreas), midgut (jejunoileum, appendix, proximal colon) and hindgut (distal colon, rectum), which influences secretory profile and behaviour

Most are non-functioning and present late with local or mass effects or with metastases; small bowel tumours characteristically incite a mesenteric desmoplastic reaction causing obstruction or ischaemia
Carcinoid syndrome develops in only a minority and usually implies hepatic metastases, or a bronchial or ovarian primary that bypasses portal clearance
Appendiceal and small rectal tumours are frequently incidental and, when small and localised, have an excellent prognosis after local resection
Grading by Ki-67 index and mitotic count (WHO G1 to G3) is central to prognosis and distinguishes well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour from poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma
Chromogranin A is the main circulating tumour marker and somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE) is the imaging modality of choice for staging
Somatostatin analogues control symptoms and slow progression, with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, targeted agents and liver-directed therapies available for advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Carcinoid (well-differentiated neuroendocrine) tumours arise from enterochromaffin and other neuroendocrine cells dispersed through the gut and bronchial epithelium. They can synthesise bioactive amines and peptides, most notably serotonin, stored in neurosecretory granules. When these mediators drain into the portal circulation they are largely inactivated by the liver, so systemic effects (carcinoid syndrome) usually appear only with hepatic metastases or extra-portal primaries. Locally, midgut tumours provoke a fibrotic desmoplastic reaction in the mesentery that can cause bowel obstruction or ischaemia. Tumour behaviour ranges from indolent low-grade lesions to more aggressive higher-grade tumours, stratified by proliferative activity.
additionalDifferentials: Adenocarcinoma of the same primary site such as bowel or lung
Lymphoma or gastrointestinal stromal tumour of the small bowel
Appendicitis or appendiceal mucocoele for appendiceal lesions
Inflammatory bowel disease or mesenteric ischaemia mimicking mesenteric involvement
Metastatic neuroendocrine tumour of unknown primary
additionalInvestigations: Chromogranin A, with 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA if functional disease is suspected
Somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE) for staging and receptor status
Multiphase contrast CT or MRI to define primary, mesenteric and hepatic disease
Endoscopy, colonoscopy or bronchoscopy for accessible primaries, with biopsy
Histology with Ki-67 index and mitotic count for WHO grading
Echocardiography if carcinoid syndrome or a raised 5-HIAA suggests cardiac involvement
FDG-PET in higher-grade tumours to assess more aggressive biology
redFlags: Small bowel obstruction or mesenteric ischaemia from the desmoplastic reaction
New carcinoid syndrome indicating likely hepatic metastases
Rapidly progressive disease or a high Ki-67 suggesting a high-grade tumour
Carcinoid heart disease with right heart failure or a new murmur
Risk of carcinoid crisis around surgery, anaesthesia or tumour manipulation
reference.prognosis: Well-differentiated, localised carcinoid tumours, especially small appendiceal and rectal lesions, have an excellent prognosis; in metastatic disease prognosis depends on grade and tumour burden but is frequently indolent, with prolonged survival achievable using modern therapies.
pitfalls: Assuming all carcinoids are benign, when higher-grade and metastatic tumours behave aggressively
Omitting Ki-67 grading, which changes prognosis and treatment
Overlooking a small bowel primary as the cause of an unexplained mesenteric mass or obstruction
Failing to give perioperative somatostatin analogue prophylaxis against carcinoid crisis
Confusing well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour with poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma, which require very different management
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System and Thoracic Tumours
ENETS Consensus Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours
management: Localised resectable disease is treated with surgical resection, ranging from local or endoscopic excision for small low-risk lesions to formal oncologic resection with regional lymphadenectomy for larger or higher-risk tumours.
Perioperative somatostatin analogue cover is mandatory before surgery, anaesthesia, or any invasive procedure in patients with functional disease to prevent carcinoid crisis.
Even with unresectable metastatic disease, resection of a symptomatic or obstructing primary (especially ileal primaries) may be pursued for symptom control.

Poorly differentiated, high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma is managed like small-cell carcinoma with platinum-based chemotherapy rather than the well-differentiated NET pathway, and should prompt urgent medical oncology referral.
Asymptomatic, newly diagnosed unresectable or metastatic low-grade disease can be actively surveilled without immediate systemic therapy.

Liver-dominant metastatic disease is managed with liver-directed options such as resection or ablation, radiofrequency or microwave ablation, transarterial embolisation or chemoembolisation, or selective liver transplantation.
Somatostatin analogues are first-line antitumour therapy for progressive metastatic midgut NETs and are also the foundation of carcinoid syndrome symptom control.
Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy targeting the somatostatin receptor is used on progression after standard-dose somatostatin analogue therapy in somatostatin-receptor-positive midgut disease.
Everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, has an established role in metastatic pancreatic NETs but a less certain, more selectively used role in midgut/small-bowel carcinoid.
Antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib have a clearer role in pancreatic NETs than in carcinoid or midgut tumours.

Interferon-alpha and cytotoxic chemotherapy are later-line or generally not recommended options for well-differentiated small bowel carcinoid, while checkpoint inhibition is not established as first-line.

Telotristat is added for diarrhoea inadequately controlled on a somatostatin analogue, alongside adjunctive measures like bile-acid binders, pancreatic enzymes, antibacterial treatment for overgrowth, and anti-motility agents.
Beta-2 agonists should be avoided for bronchospasm during flushing episodes, as they can provoke further mediator release.

Monitoring uses chromogranin A and 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA, cross-sectional and somatostatin-receptor imaging, and periodic echocardiography to screen for carcinoid heart disease, with early cardiology referral if valvular disease is found.
